0.title: How an inherited EGFR variant raises lung risk
0.caption: Study design, main result and origin of the germline EGFR T790M variant. Numbers from LoPiccolo et al., Science, 2026.
steps: Genetic data from more than 3.3 million people were searched for the rare inherited (germline) EGFR T790M variant.
Carriers were more likely to get lung cancer, a risk exceeding smoking's and several times greater in never-smokers, with no excess across 17 other cancer types.
The variant traces to a founder event in Southern Appalachia about 200–225 years ago; it is more common in the US and found in people of British, Irish and African descent.

1.title: How gene switches reshaped human joints
1.caption: Screen design and main result of the study on human-specific skeletal gene regulation. Numbers from Yan et al., Nature, 2026.
steps: 561,410 human-derived DNA changes in promoters and enhancers were tested with reporter assays in chondrocytes; 15,077 loci showed human-specific activity.
Human–ape hybrid cells, turned into osteochondral progenitors, were combined with the screen into genome-wide maps of human-specific cis-regulatory change.
The standout signal was suppressed glycosaminoglycan synthesis: human joints hold roughly 3–4× less than other apes', a selected shift that may explain joint fragility.

2.title: How VIPR RNAs read DNA in a gapped code
2.caption: How VIPR guide RNAs recognise DNA compared with CRISPR guides, and what the systems appear to do. Based on Yoon et al., Science, 2026.
steps: A CRISPR-Cas guide RNA base-pairs along one continuous stretch of its target DNA.
A VIPR RNA alternates GGY and NN motifs; only the variable NN dinucleotides specify the target, together encoding a gapped sequence on double-stranded DNA.
The Vipr protein is ancestral to the earliest CRISPR-Cas effectors; the systems look like phage-versus-phage weapons and can be reprogrammed to repress transcription.

3.title: How a brain atlas maps variants to cell types
3.caption: Design and main results of the single-nucleus eQTL atlas of the prefrontal cortex. Numbers from Zeng et al., Nature Genetics, 2026.
steps: 5.6 million nuclei were profiled from the prefrontal cortex of 1,384 donors of diverse ancestry.
Across 8 cell classes and 27 subclasses, genetic regulation was found for 14,258 genes; 981 were cell-type-specific at class level and 857 at subclass level.
Matching these signals to disease associations revealed new cell-type-specific candidate genes for Alzheimer's, schizophrenia and other disorders, invisible in bulk tissue.
